@alexbrier718  Thank you very much for giving good advise! Can you recommend a CPU? I was looking to buy a 2600X or a 2700X. My problem is :
2600X : 156€ + fan 58€
Or

author: @bert7574

text: Depends. The ryzen 2600 ( comes with wraith stealth cooler) for $130 on amazon in us vs the 2600x which is $147 and the x version comes with a better cooler (wraith spire). Same cooler is on the 2700 and then the 2700x has wraith prism.  The 2700 is $186 and the 2700x is $236. My personal rig uses a 2700 with the stock  spire cooler and stays under 55 Celsius when gaming. The 6c/12t 2600x would be just about all you really need, but if you plan to keep the cpu for a while and want the extra 2c/4t then go for the 2700 (non x) and dont bother replacing the coolers on either one. Unless you plan to do something like video editing or cad software stuff, etc. Then an upgraded cooler is a good idea. For just gaming and light work. The spire is plenty to cool the 2700 and it saves me at least $50 where I live. If I had to start from scratch building a pc again I'd go with the 2600x if new. You might find a really good deal on a 2600 used and then be able to spend the difference on actually upgrading the cooler. But if you're buying new, go 2600x or 2700 if you really want it and spend the money you were gonna spend on a cooler on other better parts or peripherals

text:
@ventzp2133  The RTX 2060 is fast enough to be able to play Battlefield V at over 60 fps with the ray-tracing (which in that case is reflections) on.
Whatever it's worth the speed trade-off is up to each and everyone but it's definitely playable. And in a non-competitive game I would prefer using it.
At-least before it wasn't good enough I'd say for the global illumination in Metro Exodus, maybe in 720p. Would I prefer 720p with rendered light rather than 1080 with global illumination? I don't know. Maybe. I would definitely take rendered light and shadows and reflections with less details from DLSS than being without them though.

Regardless of how well the RTX 2060 can handle it will be better than what the Navi card will be able too. And the games will come. Personally I wouldn't have to have an advanced game to appreciate it. Something simple like the cartoon style machines(?) demo would be fine for me too. Lots of games will use it eventually. I'd imagine just about all would want to use it completely if the hardware was capable of supporting that. But it's not today. And the games developed for the upcoming game consoles may not run well with ray-tracing even in 1080p on the RTX 2060. It's still better than the Navis though. As said.

The Navi card only offer potentially HDMI VRR support where Nvidia may have none, and that's not even one I'm sure will be true and currently it's only relevant to very few people (for monitors they will have DisplayPort so only really relevant if you game on the TV and if it supports it.) It's an advantage though just as ray-tracing and tensor cores are too.

@shido8597  I won't bother trying to find power consumption in the video so I just went to Sweclockers to check instead:
2060FE: 45/260/290 watt full system idle, average, max.
5700: 40/270/290
2060 Super: 40/265/290
5700 XT: 40/330/360

"Efficient" may be an exaggeration but yeah I'll grant you they are clearly on par with each other as far as power consumption goes. My bad. I guess I went with the rumors + high temperatures + loud noise-level and assumed they pulled more power even though 7 nm. The rest is still true. And clearly the design isn't all that good considering they pull as much power as similarly performing Nvidia cards made at 12 nm.

@twistedoracle4555  The Super card replace the old ones and have 8 GB so that's not really a point any longer. And even when it was if that was ever an issue the solution is no harder than lower texture settings until you are below 6 GB and get good performance again. Typically, with the GTX 1060 3 GB being the exception, once the VRAM amount has become an issue the card has been to slow to run those games at those settings anyway. Regardless it won't really be a valid point as the RTX 2060 is discontinued and replaced by the RTX 2060 Super now which have 8 GB of VRAM.

text:
Praise + wish + criticism:

Really nice review! Love the video structure and how the information was shown!
Somehow I feel very welcome and at home when watching one of your reviews.
Really looking forward to that Anti-Lag testing!  

Would also like to see revisiting Radeon Chill, comparing Vega and Navi.
I think also interesting would be: Limiting all cards (Vega, Navi, Turing, (+Polaris and Pascal?)) with VSync to 60fps  for the sake of comparing the efficiency when the cards don't need to clock at maximum. 
Basically,  how good is each generation at a performance level that is ... simply enough. 
I would find it very interesting to see a what remains from each offering when you normalize/remove the performance component. How does the experience compare? Power, noise, image quality, input lag, software environment....

Now, criticism: 
Often you say high value, followed by pointing out that it is the small number sitting low on the graph. 
Cost per Frame is inverted Value. I don't know why you would choose to go with this definition. 
Its not like I could say "Hm, 40fps is enough for me. Now lets pick the best value Card ... Vega 56 is 3.41$/Frame. Nice! So I can get the experience I want for 40*3.41=137.4$ by buing a Vega 56!" .... no, you can't. 
Of course, calculating Value as Performance/Price doesn't tell you much more either .... but then saying "high Value" works so much better with the visuals.
(My favorite representation would be an XY-plot (for each resolution) of average fps over price. Would exactly tell you how much you would have to spend get the desired performance. And it would nicely show diminishing returns. You did this in the Ryzen 3000 review ..... but inverted again. squint ) 

Idk, maybe I have hardware OCD or something ... Maybe I'm the only person that cares ... anyway, I would really appreciate it and I could not think of any other criticism regarding your videos.
(Ok, other than that my i7-5500u pretty much maxes out with 60fps videos and it seems kinda pointless for showing bar charts.)

I wish you guys a fun week! :)

text:
The reason for the comparatively increased power draw's when looking at the total system power draw's, is due to the higher temps and the number of components. Because of these, there are different levels in component power draw's, greater VRM losses in efficiency, and for every 10C change in component (GPU, VRAM, VRM) temps there's a 3 - 4% change in power draw.

To give an example using rough values as I don't have the cards on hand to get actual numbers:
5700 TBP = 154W GPU + ~6W misc board components + ~16W G6 = ~176W / ~0.83 (83% eff) VRM losses = ~212W + ~8W fan = ~220W TBP
2060 TBP = 170W + ~6W + ~12W = ~188W / ~0.85 = ~220W + ~6W = ~226W TBP
Then any temp differences between them will do the rest.

text: @combatantezoteric2965  It's not that unusual for 2nd and 3rd gen Ryzens to do better stock, particularly those that are already close to max OC limits (like R7 and X models). Manual OC will disable boosting, so stock can end up performing better.

text:
A few key takeaways on this review vs GN. Firstly they used different test bench and different games tested, also HU seemed to be on press drivers vs GN mentioned using release ones. Gns card seemed to be a dud at overclocking as well as he said the 5700xt was a poor overclocker and this seemed like it overclocked very well which could be bunning or likely drivers.

Then in the presentation HU did not include overclocked numbers where GN did which resulted him often comparing significantly overclocked Nvidia models vs  AMD base numbers which did not benefit from an overclock at all. This ended up with him basically showing the 2600S beating or tying 5700xt at every turn. Considering that he even said overclocking was not working with the release drivers it seems like Nvidia had a large advantage.

GN focused heavily on not liking the blower fan while HU admitted it was a bit loud but wasn't so phased by it. HU focused much less on the cooling which was adequate but not great but put in charts showing stock vs stock speeds and prices which AMD came out a definite winner.

So who was wrong? Well neither really, if you are a practical gamer who cares about price to performance and can live with a little higher noise and heat in your rig the AMD cards win hands down. If you are a hardware tweaker who wants to OC everything or want the best lowest noise and thermals. Then you may be dissapointed with these and that overclocking at least on release drivers might  not working might be a big letdown for you as well. Even though I've disagreed with HU on a lot of other issues I personally think HU got it right here. But many others may say the blower and possible lack of OC potential are deal breakers for them. And if that's true for them they aren't really wrong either. All comes down to what's important for you in the end.

Nvidia remains the best-of-the-best with its RTX 2080 Ti, but I know majority of gamers don't care about this.

Looks like the RX 5700 finally is direct competition to the GTX 1080, finally something to properly surpass the old R9 290/390X and bring competition, even if it took them 3 years (also its cousins RTX 2070 and 2060-Super).

Whereas the RX 5700xt is direct competition to the GTX 1080 Ti, and is somewhat less impressive, but its only 2 years behind (also its cousins RTX 2080 and 2080-Super).

And now suddenly, the rumours about next year's PS5 and Xbox V having graphical performance that's around the GTX 1080 is not looking like wishful-thinking but actual reality. So it looks like we can expect proper 4K/High Settings/60fps-FreeSync on the upcoming consoles for both lighter games (F1 2019) and heavy games (FarCry New Dawn).

text:
@cereal6675  
I think both consoles are targeting a unified memory system like they did with the PS4 Pro and Xbox One X. 

So there's going to be 32GB's of GDDR6 to play with. Some of that will be left unavailable, others will be dedicated for multitasking, CPU, and the GPU.

So no, there looks like enough performance there to do more than 4K/Medium/30fps... moreso like True 4K-HDR/High/60fps-FreeSync. So if you built a Gaming PC in 2016, it will now have a match, even if it is 4 years later.

The reason why I'm excited is because PC Games follow in the shadows of their console partners. If the consoles are too weak, we get sloppy ports. And this time its shaping to be a proper generational improvement and not a dumb Pro-Plus upgrade. It's as big of an upgrade as going from say 2005 Xbox 360 to 2013 Xbox One, as it is to go from 2013 Xbox One to 2020 Xbox V..... or in other words, the 2013 consoles were a huge letdown for us enthusiasts, since we expected something closer to a PS4 Pro hardware at the time, but didn't get it until 2016.
